messages.content: Write a post about what a software company learned from a year of remote work. Around 250 words.

**Twelve Months Without an Office**

We shut the office in March last year and left everyone to work it out. Here's what we understand now that we didn't then.

Productivity wasn't the first casualty. The hallway was. Nobody had accounted for the fact that half our decisions got made in the twenty seconds after a meeting broke up, while people were still standing there. Those decisions didn't migrate to Slack. They simply stopped, and we found out weeks later when two teams shipped rival versions of the same feature.

The remedy was dull: a standing thirty-minute call every Tuesday, no agenda. People grumbled about it for two months. Then they started protecting it.

Second lesson: writing is a skill, and most of us weren't good at it. A fuzzy Slack message that a glance across the desk would have sorted out now burns someone's afternoon. So we began asking people to write longer messages, which sounds like the wrong direction until you tally the round trips it prevents.

Hiring got easier. Onboarding got worse. We can recruit anywhere, and we've got people across six time zones. But a new engineer used to pick up how we work by sitting next to people who already knew. That transfer doesn't survive video. We had to write down things nobody had ever bothered to write down, and the writing took months.

Would we go back? No. But we'd admit the office was doing work we never noticed until we lost it.

output:
**A Year With No Office**

We closed the office last March and told everyone to figure it out. Twelve months on, here's what we know now that we didn't then.

The first thing we lost wasn't output. It was the corridor. None of us had registered that a good half of our decisions got settled in the twenty seconds after a meeting broke up, while everyone was still on their feet. Those decisions never made it into Slack. They just stopped happening, and we found out weeks later when two teams shipped competing versions of the same feature.

Our fix was boring: a thirty-minute call every Tuesday with nothing on the agenda. People complained about it for two months. Then they started defending it.

The second thing: writing is a skill, and most of us were bad at it. A vague Slack message that a look across the desk would once have cleared up now eats somebody's afternoon. So we started asking people to write longer messages. That sounds backwards until you count the round trips it saves.

Hiring got easier. Onboarding got worse. We can recruit anywhere now, and we have people in six time zones. But a new engineer used to absorb how we work by sitting beside people who already did. Video doesn't carry that. We had to write down things nobody had ever thought to write down, and the writing took months.

Would we reopen? No. But the office was doing work for us that we never saw until it was gone.
